headline: Harmony is sounds working together—multiple notes creating richer textures than any could alone
universal_truth: Combination creates emergence; together, elements can produce what none could individually
fun_facts: The physics of harmony relates to simple ratios—octaves are exactly 2:1 frequency ratios
Western and Eastern musical traditions developed different harmonic systems independently
Dissonance isn't 'bad'—it creates tension that makes resolution feel satisfying
discussion_questions: Why do some note combinations sound 'pleasant' and others 'clashing'?
How is musical harmony like other forms of cooperation?
What in your life creates harmony when combined?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: One note is melody. Add a second note at the same time and something new appears: harmony. Some combinations sound peaceful, others tense, others rich. Multiple sounds interacting create something none could produce alone—musical chemistry.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Why do some note combinations sound 'right' and others 'wrong'? Is harmony just cultural preference, or is there something deeper?
cliff.prompt: Why do some harmonies sound pleasant?

options.text: Pleasant harmonies have simple mathematical ratios between their frequencies—our brains process them more easily
options.response: Yes. Octaves (2:1), fifths (3:2), and fourths (4:3) have simple ratios our brains recognize as 'consonant.' More complex ratios create 'dissonance'—not bad, just tension.

options.text: We learn which harmonies are pleasant from our musical culture
options.response: Culture shapes preference, but the mathematical basis of consonance appears universal...

q1.title: Math in Music
q1.script: Pythagoras discovered harmony's mathematics 2,500 years ago. Notes that sound good together have frequencies in simple ratios. Music isn't arbitrary—it's physics and math translated into emotion. Beauty has structure.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Math in Music"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Tension and Release
q2.script: Dissonance isn't error—it's tool. Composers use dissonance to create tension, then resolve to consonance for satisfaction. Without dissonance, harmony is flat. The journey between tension and release is what makes music emotional.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Cultural Variations
q3.script: Different cultures developed different harmonic systems. Western music emphasizes thirds and triads. Indian ragas use different intervals. Middle Eastern music uses microtones Western music ignores. Harmony is universal; specific harmonies are cultural.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Combination creates emergence. Harmony teaches that together, elements can produce what none could individually. The right combinations make the whole greater than the sum of parts.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 166. Tomorrow, we'll explore machines that make music—electronic instruments. Until then, listen for harmony in music—and in life.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Harmony Recognition - Hear the Blend
growTrack.activity: Listen to a song with vocals and instruments. Try to hear how sounds blend—which notes support the melody? Where does tension build? Where does it resolve? Harmony is agreement; notice what happens when sounds work together.
